name: Yasuaki Shimizu
discourse_profile: Sound as texture moving through space. Shimizu's central preoccupation is the physical behavior of sound in an environment — 'What captivates me is the texture of sound, how it moves within a space, and my relationship with time as the sound floats through it.' A childhood experience hearing thousands of insects creating 'a wave of electronic sound' near Mt. Fuji seeded this orientation. His studio method is deliberately unpremeditated — 'My style when it came to making music was to go into the recording studio with virtually nothing prepared, and put it all together from the ground up' — visualizing the mixing console as a 'miniature garden' where harmonics dance. He drew on African and Southeast Asian music but explicitly rejected imitation: 'I had no interest in imitating that genius; I perceived it more as a way to expand my own sonic vocabulary.' This unclassifiability was Mariah's deliberate position — record shops filed the albums in jazz and buyers complained 'this isn't jazz,' while radio listeners couldn't find the right section. His Bach cello suites project made the spatial philosophy explicit — recording solo saxophone in quarries, mines, and palazzos to 'play the space' as a resonating instrument. Jazz training (Ornette Coleman, Rahsaan Roland Kirk) gave him improvisational reflexes, but he was equally drawn to the heta-uma aesthetic — 'the fluctuation, the twistedness, the muddiness' of The Flying Lizards. His basic approach, established during Utakata no Hibi and Kakashi in the early '80s, has remained fundamentally unaltered: take a simple theme and challenge it through improvisation.
